en: The Sūtra on the Auspicious Night, Spoken by the Buddha. One fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the Bamboo Grove Park in the city of Rājagṛha.
Not far from there, a bhikṣu was dwelling by the side of a hot spring.
At that time, a deva of handsome appearance and exquisite radiance approached the bhikṣu after the first watch of the night had passed.
The majestic radiance of that deva was perfectly circular and brilliantly resplendent;
it illuminated the entire hot spring, pervading it everywhere.
Joining his palms in reverent salutation, he sat to one side.
He said to the bhikṣu, "Venerable sir,
have you perhaps previously heard the *Sujātā-sūtra*?
The bhikṣu replied, "I have never heard such a sūtra."
He asked the deva again, "Do you know beforehand?
The deva replied, "I do not know either.
The bhikṣu asked, "Who is it that knows?"
The deity said, "The Unsurpassed Compassionate Father resides in the Bamboo Grove Monastery.
You should now go there to inquire;
you should practice according to what the Buddha has taught."
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn,
that bhikṣu went to the place where the World-Honored One was and prostrated at his feet.
Standing to one side, he addressed the World-Honored One in white words:
"Last night, after the first watch had passed,
there was a deva who came to my place."
A brilliant light shone throughout the hot springs,
and it asked me:
"Virtuous one, have you perhaps heard the *Bhadrakarātrī-sūtra* before?"
I said, "I have not heard of it.
I asked that deva, "Did you know of it beforehand?
He replied, "I did not know."
I asked again, "Who knows?
He replied, "The Unsurpassed Father is at the Bamboo Grove Monastery;
you may go there and ask him."
"I shall carry out what the Buddha has taught.
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.
It is for this reason that I have come here to question the World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Do you recognize that deva?
They replied, "We do not recognize him.
"You should now know," he said, "that he is a sublime and excellent son of the gods from the Heaven of the Thirty-three, a great general of majestic power named Candana."
"Out of a desire to benefit all sentient beings,
he has come to awaken you by inquiring about the name of this sutra.
At that time, the bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I now wish to hear the *Sujātā-sūtra*.
I pray only that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will explain it for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
This *Rātripratisaṃyukta-sūtra* possesses great merit.
Anyone who hears it will be able to sever the afflictions and swiftly realize awakening.
You should listen attentively and apply your minds with the utmost care.
I shall explain this for you:
one should not pursue past phenomena,
nor should one long for future phenomena.
"Do not give rise to defiled attachment toward any phenomena of the present.
A practitioner who acts in this way is called truly liberated.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
One should not dwell on the past, nor long for the future;
within the present moment, one should observe all things according to the Dharma.
Since the deluded mind is difficult to dispel, the wise person should skillfully contemplate.
"You should practice with diligent haste;
who knows if by tomorrow you will be followed by the hosts of the King of Death?
Therefore, I, the Muni, have now recited this Sūtra of the Auspicious Night."
May all sentient beings always aspire to be free from suffering and attain peace and happiness;
may they refrain from all unwholesome deeds and constantly cultivate every kind of virtue.
At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to benefit all living beings, [spoke thus].
May they attain peace and happiness throughout the long night, be free from all obstacles and afflictions,
increase their roots of goodness in every place of rebirth,
always encounter the Triple Gem, and never fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, this dhāraṇī is spoken:
Tadyathā | vini pare |
Vadama dāṃdhe maniṇi ṭi ṭi ṭi ṭi kauri gandhali.
Caṇḍāli mātaṅgi saralante mohurati śapali kārāpaki.
Cāvari mahācāvari pucche kṣule nini minimi nime.
Kṛtani svāhā saṃyate divyaṃta āṣāḍhe.
Naragati-bhaṅga-sukhāpaya-kalpabuddha-droha.
*Kāpota-puṭa-dhāni svāhā*.
If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, or other sons and daughters of good family...
In this *Suvikrāntavikrāmi-paripṛcchā-sūtra*,
if one reads, recites, receives, upholds, makes offerings to, and honors even a single verse or a single mantra, [one shall obtain immeasurable merit].
One who clearly understands its meaning and expounds it for others should know that,
at all times, this person will be free from calamities,
as well as from unjust misfortunes and all forms of decline and affliction.
They are able to know the events of seven past lifetimes,
never forget the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*),
and are certain to proceed upon the true path to *nirvāṇa*.
If there are good men or good women who receive,
uphold, read, and recite this Bhadrakarātrī Sūtra,
in whatever place they are born in future lives, [they shall...]
One will certainly attain the knowledge of past lives and shall constantly experience noble, peaceful, and happy states.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
This person, at all times, shall have no cause for unjust or violent harm;
by performing deeds in accordance with the seasons, they shall forever be free from untimely death.
Protecting all sentient beings, may they be freed from illness, sorrow, and fear.
Inauspiciousness and evil dreams shall cease; on perilous paths one shall always be secure and at ease.
Whether man or woman, those who wear and uphold this sutra will be respected by those endowed with noble marks, and all their aspirations shall be fulfilled.
If there be any unwholesome deeds of body,
speech, or mind, by the power of this sutra, they shall never result in evil retribution;
nor shall there be harm from water, fire, kings, thieves, lightning, thunder, poison, or injury.
When enemies are engaged in battle, by reciting this sutra one shall be liberated from them all.
Furthermore, there is a vidyā-mantra; if one is able to read and recite it, at all times it will increase all that is wholesome and extinguish all evils.
Then he spoke the mantra, saying:
Tadyathā | nirmi nimindare |
Cillukālocini cilluśuladharini aṅkubi.
Cchili ti nu le ku du guṇḍi ku du kuccha.
Kṛtigrāmaṇī, protect,
protect me, [Name], in all places of terror and in all places of sickness and suffering.
In all situations of sorrow, grief, and affliction; in all situations involving venomous insects and poisons;
in all situations involving malevolent spirits, curses, and incantations;
and in all situations involving kings, thieves, water, and fire.
In all places of terror caused by fierce beasts,
in all places of slander, defamation, and litigation,
and in all places of strife and contention with enemies.
In all instances of bodily and mental misconduct,
in all instances of the four faults of vocal karma,
and in all instances of calamity, distress, and peril.
And may the Vajrapāṇi deity constantly protect me, [Name], along with all my retinue. Svāhā. Furthermore, he spoke this mantra:
Tadyathā | hiri hiri miri miri piśācipraṇa śapharici svāhā. At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken this sutra, [entered parinirvāṇa].

At that time, those bhikṣus and the great assembly—including humans, devas, the eight classes of beings, and various spirits—were all filled with great joy; they accepted the teaching with faith and practiced it accordingly.
Thus concludes the *Bhadrarātrī-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
